title: Neural Darwinism
program_note:
The term “Neural Darwinism” relates to the theory in neuro-psychology that at birth a human being has many more neurons and neural connections than it would ever be able to use, most of which die off or disappear quite quickly.  The only neurons and neural connections that survive are those which have been reinforced through repeated use.  Hence, there is a neural “survival of the fittest,” or “Neural Darwinism.”  This trend towards simplification and familiarity-through-repetition, however, raises the question of how, afterwards, there can arise the complex and biologically unprecedented thoughts that set human beings off from the rest of the animal kingdom?

Neural Darwinism can be thought of as a musical answer to that question, which in the process becomes a sort of musical “life of a brain.”  In the first movement, Neural Darwinism, there is a gradual increase in the amount and apparent randomness of the sound produced by the orchestra; these sounds get threshed out by a Darwinian “survival of the fittest” process, leaving behind nothing but a perfect fifth.  This perfect fifth gets repeated until, through the interactions of the overtone series of the two pitches that make up the P5, other pitches and intervals get introduced; juxtaposition and new interactions combine to produce the complexity referred to above.

This complexity increases, approaching the density of sound of measures 26-39, until we pass into the second movement, entitled Sensory Overload, in which there is a straight-forward programmatic representation of nerve impulses being transmitted up -- and down -- the neural pathways.  Probably another acceptable title would be slow epileptic seizure.  Gradually the individual notes that go into the long upwards and downwards lines are sustained — or resound, producing residual harmonies that take us into the third movement.

Entitled Transcendental Consciousness, in the third movement chords — harmonies — throb and repeat, in what can be thought of as a verticalization of all of the melodies and lines heard previously.   In essence the melodies have been simplified and condensed into a small series of throbbing, fading and phasing harmonies.

This work was conceived during the summer of 1994, and was written from September to December, 1995.  The three “movements,” or parts of the work, flow directly from one to the next without pause.  The total duration of the work is approximately 10’00”; the durations of the individual parts are, respectively, 4’55”, 1’50”, and 3’15”.

David S. Lefkowitz

December 21, 1995

Rochester, NY
